<p class="eyebrow">Figures</p>

# Layout, drawing and typography

::: {.doc-lead}
Arrange panels, draw annotations, and control the details of a figure.
:::

## Everyday editing {#everyday-editing}

**The pointer.** In the Figure and Slide editors the pointer is Flux's own: by default a
**classic arrow** in Figma's style — a pink, slightly leaning arrowhead with a deep indigo
outline — and it is one mark that changes form rather than a set of unrelated system arrows.
Over an object's edge or corner it becomes a double-headed resize arrow in the same colours,
just outside a corner a curved rotate arrow, with a small **+** while **Alt** is duplicating,
and it keeps that form for the whole drag. Paper, Reader and Library keep the system's
cursors; text fields keep the I-beam and pan keeps the hand.

**Settings → General → Cursor** tunes the pointer with a live preview. **Style** chooses
**Classic arrow** or **Crosshair**. The arrow has fill and outline colours, size, outline
width, corner rounding, shadow and tilt; **Press on click** adds a subtle tip-led depression on
the canvas while the button is down, with **Press depth** (1.25× by default) and **Return
time** (80 ms by default), and **Click to try the press** lets you feel a change. The
**crosshair** is a precise cross with a gap at the centre, so the pixel you point at is never
covered; its colour follows the surface (dark ink over paper and other light surfaces,
paper-white over the dark canvas and chrome), with its own colours, stroke, optional halo,
centre mark, hover dot and press contraction, and **Adaptive**, **Outlined** and **Accent**
presets. Either style can hand the resize, rotate and move states back to the system's own
cursors.

**Selecting and moving.** Click an object to select it; a path, line or hollow shape is
selected by clicking on or near its stroke. Once selected, its **bounding box is the handle**:
drag from anywhere inside the box — an open path's empty interior, a hollow ellipse's middle,
the gaps of a group, even over a plot the path annotates — to move it, and a click there keeps
it selected (a click on an object lying beneath the selection selects that object instead; an
object drawn on top of the selection still wins its own click). A drag has to travel a few
pixels before anything moves, so a shaky click never nudges. With several objects selected, a
click on one of them selects just that one; a drag still moves them all.

**Resizing and rotating.** The selection shows four corner handles. Drag a **corner** to resize
both axes, or grab **anywhere along an edge** to resize that axis alone — the edge follows your
drag from wherever you took hold of it, and snaps to neighbouring edges, centres and guides
the way a move does. **Shift** keeps the proportions (from an edge it grows about the opposite
edge's middle), **Alt** resizes about the centre (press or release it mid-drag and the box
follows at once), and the live **W × H** readout under the box shows the size as you go.
Thin objects — a scale bar, a one-line label — have no edge bands across their short side, so
their whole body stays grabbable; their corners still resize them from the outside. To
rotate, drag the knob above the box or simply drag from **just outside any corner**;
**Shift** snaps to 15°. **Ctrl+drag** a handle or edge of an image or plot to crop instead
(on a plot, **Ctrl** just inside the edge still picks the part under the pointer). Images and
plots resize freely by an edge, so use a corner or **Shift** when the proportions matter. What
happens to a plot's axes and type when you resize it is in [Resizing a plot](#resizing-a-plot).

**Moving between figures and the rest.** Drag to move (with smart snapping and alignment
guides), arrows to nudge, **Alt+drag** to duplicate, **Shift+drag** to constrain to an axis. To
move something to a **different figure**, just drag it there: the figure under the pointer
lights up, and releasing puts the selection into that figure where you dropped it (groups and
panel captions come along; one Undo brings it back). **Ctrl+X** cuts, **Ctrl+C** copies and
**Ctrl+V** pastes, so a cut in one figure and a paste in another is the keyboard way to do the
same thing. **Ctrl+G** groups (**Ctrl+Shift+G** ungroups), **]** brings to front and **[**
sends to back (with **Ctrl** they move one step), **Shift+H** / **Shift+V** flip, **Delete**
removes, **Escape** cancels whatever you're midway through. To line things up, space them
evenly or reflow them into a grid, press **A** for [Align & Arrange](#align-and-arrange).

## Align & Arrange {#align-and-arrange}

Select objects and press **A** to open **Align & Arrange** beside them, with Align active;
**Alt+T** opens it with Arrange active. Both panes stay visible — click a pane or one of its
controls to activate it, or press **Space** while the tool surface has focus to switch. The
panel works the same way on slides.

<figure class="doc-figure doc-clip"><video poster="/assets/media/docs/clips/align-arrange.png" width="1400" height="1000" muted loop playsinline autoplay controls preload="metadata" aria-label="Three plots at different heights are aligned to their top edge with one click, then spaced evenly with Distribute horizontal spacing."><source src="/assets/media/docs/clips/align-arrange.mp4" type="video/mp4"></video><figcaption>Align top, then even horizontal spacing: each click is one undo step and the panel stays open.</figcaption></figure>

<figure class="doc-figure"><a href="/assets/media/docs/figure-align-arrange.png" data-enlarge data-caption="Press A with objects selected. Align is active on the left; Arrange stays visible on the right, and Space switches between them."><img src="/assets/media/docs/figure-align-arrange.png" alt="The Align &amp; Arrange panel open beside three selected plots: the Align pane with its six edge and centre buttons and their key hints, Even spacing, Match plot area and Plot spines controls, and the Arrange pane with Row, Grid and Column, spacing and Keep fixed." width="2800" height="2000" loading="lazy"></a><figcaption>Press <strong>A</strong> with objects selected. Align is active on the left; Arrange stays visible on the right, and <strong>Space</strong> switches between them.</figcaption></figure>

**Align.** Click an alignment button or use **W/A/S/D** for top/left/bottom/right; **H**
aligns X centres along a vertical line and **V** aligns Y centres along a horizontal line.
**To** chooses what you align to: **Selection bounds**, a named **Reference object**, or the
**Figure** frame (one selected object aligns to the figure). **Even spacing → Horizontal /
Vertical** distributes three or more objects, keeping the outermost ones fixed. Each alignment
is one undo step and the panel stays open. A plot with parts hidden in X-ray aligns and
arranges by its visible outline. Without the panel, **Alt+A / Alt+W / Alt+S / Alt+D** align
left/top/bottom/right and **Alt+H / Alt+V** centre horizontally/vertically.

**Plot spines.** For semantic plots, the Align pane adds **X spines** (**X**), which aligns
horizontal axes, and **Y spines** (**Y**), which aligns vertical axes. The **Reference** plot
stays fixed. Whole groups move together, annotations included. For multi-panel plots, open
**Plot, panel & spine choices** to identify the intended axis. Unavailable spines are explained
in the pane, and ordinary alignment remains available. These commands move plots without
changing their domains, sizes or internal geometry. **Match plot area** sits in the same pane
and changes the plots' sizes so their data areas match; see [Resizing a plot](#resizing-a-plot).

**Arrange.** An existing row, column or simple grid keeps its order and internal offsets while
uneven gaps are tidied, and a regular arrangement stays where it is. An ambiguous selection gets
a **Suggested grid** preview. **Row**, **Grid** and **Column** reflow the selection into centred
cells; **A** toggles row/column, **G** chooses a balanced grid, and **D** / **F** add or remove
rows.

**Gap guides and spacing.** Selecting an already evenly spaced row, column or simple grid shows
pink gap guides without opening the panel; this recognition leaves the objects unchanged, and
ambiguous overlaps show no guides. Drag a guide to edit the spacing as one undo step. In the
panel, drag a gap guide to adjust all gaps on that axis, or enter, scroll or scrub a value in
the spacing field (**Horizontal gap** / **Vertical gap**, or **Column gap** / **Row gap** in a
grid). Right/down increases spacing, left/up decreases it; **Shift** adjusts faster and **Alt**
more finely. Spacing is signed: negative gaps overlap objects, which is what stacked traces or
waveforms want, and there is no zero floor — very negative spacing can move successive tracks
past one another while they keep their members, sizes and stacking order. Grid gaps measure the
space between column and row tracks, so smaller objects can have more visible clearance within
their cells.

**Keep fixed** chooses which edge or centre stays in place while the spacing changes; a grid
offers nine anchor points. Click the small pin on the selection to open the same chooser
without opening the panel. Centre is the initial default, and your choice stays selected across
selections and tool visits in the current session. **1 / 2 / 3** chooses start/centre/end on
the gap axis you are editing or hovering (numeric fields keep normal typing). Choosing a
different anchor moves nothing until you change the spacing, and the fixed point always uses
the actual selection bounds, overlap included.

**Enter** or **Apply** keeps the Arrange preview as one undo step. **Escape** cancels the
current drag or field edit first; another **Escape** restores the arrangement from when you
entered. Switching back to Align keeps the arrangement. Input fields keep normal typing —
**Enter** accepts a field — and keyboard-focused buttons keep their normal **Enter**/**Space**
activation. Middle-button and wheel navigation stay available between edits. These tools set
ordinary object positions; they do not create an automatic layout that later moves newly added
objects.

From the command line, `flux arrange` takes `--mode tidy|reflow`, signed `--gap-x` /
`--gap-y` and start/centre/end anchors, and `flux align-plot-spines` aligns spines to a
reference ([command reference](/docs/commands.html#verb-reference)).

## The property menu {#property-menu}

<figure class="doc-figure doc-figure-compact"><a href="/assets/media/docs/figure-property-menu.png" data-enlarge data-caption="Press F for the selected object’s geometry and axis-view controls. The blue key labels let you work without moving the pointer."><img src="/assets/media/docs/figure-property-menu.png" alt="Native property menu with geometry, content scale and axis-view controls." width="906" height="1078" loading="lazy"></a><figcaption>Press F for the selected object’s geometry and axis-view controls. The blue key labels let you work without moving the pointer. Click to enlarge.</figcaption></figure>

Press **F** with anything selected for the **property menu**, the fastest way to edit with one
hand on the keyboard and one on the mouse. It opens **beside the selection**, never on top of it
(when nothing fits, it takes the side that covers the least), and lays its groups out in narrow
columns, each row a key and a name over its control, so nothing scrolls. Opening a larger picker
repositions the menu when needed to keep the selection clear.

Every hotkey is a **left-hand key**: `1`–`6`, `q` `w` `e` `r` `t`, `a` `d` `g` and
`z` `x` `c` `v` `b`, plus `h` for a plot's **content scale** or a text's **letter spacing** and
`n` for **paragraph spacing**. Your right hand stays on the mouse:

1. Press the key to **arm** the row.
2. Roll the **mouse wheel** anywhere on the screen to adjust it. A slow roll moves one step per
   notch, a flick moves fast and a trackpad scrubs; hold **Shift** for ×10 or **Alt** for ×0.1.
   **↑/↓** step too, and typed digits replace the value.
3. Press **Space** or **Enter** to apply, or **Escape** to revert.

A choice such as font or alignment expands its options inline (wheel, **w/a/s/d**, **1–9**, or
click).

Hovering any numeric row and rolling the wheel edits it directly, so
the menu works with the mouse alone as well; **s** searches the properties. It carries the
essentials (position, size with **aspect lock**, rotation, opacity) plus the deep cuts: dashed
strokes with dash/gap control, **arrowheads** on lines *and* open paths (filled or V-line,
sized, with round/flat/square caps), **corner radius** on rectangles *and* paths,
no-fill/no-stroke, separate **fill opacity** (**b**) and **stroke opacity** (**t**) — each
independent of the object's **opacity**, which multiplies both — text styling — and **save as
preset** for anything you want to reuse. The
right rail carries the same properties (fill, stroke and text colours with their palette
names, sizes, stroke widths, arrowheads), so the menu is a choice, not a requirement.

## Colours and colormaps {#colours-and-colormaps}

A colour row opens the **palette** — every row on one line, the whole grid in view — with the
full **spectrum** beside it (a saturation/value square and a hue bar, seeded from the current
colour), a hex field and an **eyedropper**; hovering a swatch previews it live, a click
applies it, and a drag on the square previews until you let go. The hex field and spectrum
follow the preview. The opacity slider under the spectrum is the *picked paint's* own
opacity — a fill picker sets the fill's, a stroke picker the stroke's (a text colour sets the
object's opacity) — and shows the selection's current value (or **mixed**).
Releasing the hue or opacity slider applies that adjustment and keeps the picker open so
you can continue tuning the colour.

The eyedropper samples a colour from your screen. On Linux it uses your desktop's
colour picker; **Escape** cancels without changing your artwork. If screen picking
is unavailable, Flux offers a magnified view labelled **Pick from Flux window**,
which samples only this window. A completed pick is one undoable change.
**Escape** or clicking outside dismisses an unchosen preview; an incomplete hex stays editable
until you finish it.

The palette comes in
**collections** — Flexoki (the default), ColorBrewer, Paul Tol's colour sets, and your
project's own imported palette — as tabs above the grid; **Shift+Tab** cycles them. **Tab**
switches the grid to the **colormaps**: every map fluxplot ships (matplotlib, Crameri's
Scientific colour maps, Paul Tol, cmasher), by collection and by type, each with a preview
bar — pick a map and hover along its bar to take the colour at that position, **r** reverses
it. Or take the *whole* map: **x** or **y** (or the *along x* / *along y* buttons under the bar)
lays it across the element as a **gradient** along that axis — x left→right, y bottom→top — for
a shape's fill or stroke, a line's or arrow's stroke (arrowheads included), or a text's glyphs.
The map's colours are stored on the element itself, so the gradient travels into every export
(SVG, PNG, TIFF), headless render and exported deck exactly as drawn;
the menu chip and the Inspector swatch show the map and name it (`crameri.batlow · along y`),
and picking any plain swatch returns the element to a solid colour. Plot *parts* take solid
colours only. **Settings → Figure → Colour pickers** chooses which palette and colormap
collection a picker opens on.

## Numeric fields and layers {#numeric-fields-and-layers}

Numeric fields accept expressions such as `240/2` and display fractional values even when
the normal wheel increment is a whole unit. Drag a field’s label to scrub, or click
its input and type. A scrub or a continuous text/property edit is one undo step; **Escape**
cancels the current preview. Mixed selections show **Mixed** and how many objects a property
can change. Locked or hidden objects, including members of a locked or hidden group, stay
unchanged while you edit the rest of a selection.

In **Layers**, **Ctrl+click** (**⌘+click** on macOS) toggles objects and **Shift+click** selects a range. With a row
focused, **↑/↓** moves through the list, **Home/End** reaches either end, **Shift+↑/↓** extends
the selection, and **F2** renames. A group opens or closes with **→/←**. Locks inherited from
a parent group explain which group must be unlocked.

## Resizing a figure {#resizing-a-figure}

Click the figure’s title above its frame, then drag an edge or corner of the frame. The
handles stay the same size on screen as you zoom. **Shift** preserves the frame’s original
aspect ratio. The Inspector shows the new dimensions during the drag; **Escape** restores
the original boundary, and a completed resize is one undo step.

Resizing the frame changes the export boundary. Your plots, text and shapes retain their
size and world position. Moving a left or top edge moves the boundary around the artwork;
elements and ruler guides adjust their local coordinates to stay in place. Artwork outside
the new frame remains in the project and reappears if you enlarge the boundary again.
Dragging the title still moves the whole figure. Slides use a shared deck stage size.

## Resizing a plot {#resizing-a-plot}

Plots saved with fluxplot 0.4 or later include measured layout information. Drag a plot's edge
or corner, or type its width and height in the Inspector, to **Reflow** it: the axes and data
areas change size, numeric ticks are recomputed, and text, strokes and markers keep their
physical point sizes — the way changing a figure's size in matplotlib does, without Python.
**Native size** (in the Inspector's **Layout** controls) restores the dimensions from Python. A
deliberate size chosen in Flux survives regeneration; an untouched plot follows the new Python
size.

<figure class="doc-figure doc-figure-compact"><a href="/assets/media/docs/figure-plot-layout.png" data-enlarge data-caption="The Inspector’s plot section: Reflow or Stretch, the Layout status, the printed size and Native size."><img src="/assets/media/docs/figure-plot-layout.png" alt="The Inspector for a selected plot: width and height, a Layout switch between Reflow and Stretch with the status Exact, the plot’s size in inches beside a Native size button, Axis view limits, Content scale, Dissections, and a Sticks to section." width="496" height="1240" loading="lazy"></a><figcaption>The Inspector’s plot section: <strong>Reflow</strong> or <strong>Stretch</strong>, the Layout status, the printed size and <strong>Native size</strong>.</figcaption></figure>

<figure class="doc-figure doc-clip"><video poster="/assets/media/docs/clips/reflow-resize.png" width="1400" height="1000" muted loop playsinline autoplay controls preload="metadata" aria-label="A fluxplot line plot is dragged narrower by its right edge: the axes and data area shrink, tick labels re-space, and the title, legend and tick text keep their size."><source src="/assets/media/docs/clips/reflow-resize.mp4" type="video/mp4"></video><figcaption>Drag an edge and a fluxplot ≥ 0.4 plot reflows: axes and data follow, text and strokes keep their point sizes, and the status reads Exact.</figcaption></figure>

**Legends** wrap onto more rows when they need more room, keeping their labels and swatches at
their original size where possible: a one-row legend wraps left to right like text, and a
multi-column legend drops columns. A legend that still cannot fit shrinks together with its
frame; a titled legend keeps its composition and shrinks as a unit. Shaded confidence bands
follow the axes like the lines they surround. Returning to a wider plot restores the original
legend layout.

**Reflow, Stretch and the Layout status.** The Inspector's **Layout** controls offer
**Reflow** and **Stretch**, the previous behaviour, in which the whole picture scales. The
status line beneath them says whether the result is **Exact**, **Reflowed**, **Approximate** or
**Stretch**, with a reason — "regenerate with fluxplot ≥ 0.4 to reflow", "polar axes not
supported", "ticks crowded", "labels fixed in source" and so on. Legacy plots need one
regeneration to enable reflow. Polar plots, 3D, subfigures, compressed layout and unsupported
transforms use Stretch with a named reason. Date, category and custom ticks keep their source
positions and labels. Extremely small sizes may crowd decorations; enlarge the plot when the
status reports this.

**Content scale** (or the **K** scale tool) is the other dial: it changes the physical size of
text, strokes and markers within the chosen box. Crop boundaries remain figure fractions during
reflow. Pictures without text or lines, such as a PNG inside an SVG, have nothing for content
scale to change, so the Inspector explains this instead of showing the field; resize the box to
make them bigger.

**Hidden parts.** Hiding plot parts in [X-ray](/docs/plot-editing.html#x-ray) tightens the
selection and hover outline around the remaining visible content. The plot keeps its saved
dimensions, so showing those parts restores its original frame. Selection, dragging, snapping,
Align & Arrange and resize previews use the visible bounds; cropping continues to work against
the saved plot frame.

**Match plot area.** Select several reflow-capable plots and use **Match plot area → Height /
Width / Both** in the Align pane of [Align & Arrange](#align-and-arrange) to match their data
areas in one undo step. The reference is the plot chosen in the pane; otherwise the first
selected plot. Then **X spines** / **Y spines** can align their reflowed spines. Aspect
constraints and infeasible sizes are reported. A single panel picked in X-ray scopes that
plot's data area for Match; other selected plots use their full panel union. Locked or
excluded plots cannot be changed by Match.

From the command line, `flux resize-plot` resizes a plot's figsize, `flux set-plot-layout-mode
--mode auto|stretch` chooses reflow or stretch, and `flux match-plot-areas --dimension
height|width|both` matches data areas ([command reference](/docs/commands.html#verb-reference)).

## Drawing {#drawing}

The shape tools do what you expect; the **pen** (P) is placement-assisted: click to place
points; a ring appears when you're close enough to your first point to **close** the shape;
**Shift** constrains segments to 0/45/90°; dashed guides snap to alignments with earlier
nodes, and tick marks snap **equal edge lengths** — perfect squares and 45-45-90 triangles
from sloppy clicks. **Enter** finishes an open curve; while the background grid is showing,
the pen snaps to its vertices.

**Double-click a path** (or press **Enter** on it) to edit its nodes. Inside node-edit:
**v** moves nodes (**Shift+drag** constrains along the axes or the flanking tangents),
**p** continues drawing — connect to an endpoint to extend or merge the path — **d** deletes
nodes, and **Ctrl+drag** on a segment **bends** it. The Inspector's *Closed path* checkbox
opens or closes any path.

## Connectors and labels that stick {#connectors-and-labels}

A line or arrow (**L** / **Shift+L**) drawn from one shape to another **sticks** to both: a
dashed outline shows the shape an end will stick to, and dragging one of its ends onto a shape
sticks that end. A filled end handle marks a stuck end. On a shape the end meets its outline,
facing the other end; on a plot, an image, a 3D model or a video it stays exactly where you
released it (hold **Ctrl** as you release to keep the exact spot on a shape too). Move a shape
and its connectors and labels follow it, live while you drag. A connector never points
backwards: as the shapes close in it thins out, and while they overlap it is hidden.

<figure class="doc-figure doc-clip"><video poster="/assets/media/docs/clips/sticky-connector.png" width="1400" height="1000" muted loop playsinline autoplay controls preload="metadata" aria-label="Two rectangles are drawn, an arrow is drawn from one to the other with a dashed outline showing the shape it will stick to, and when the second rectangle is dragged away the arrow follows it."><source src="/assets/media/docs/clips/sticky-connector.mp4" type="video/mp4"></video><figcaption>An arrow drawn from one shape to another sticks to both; move a shape and the arrow follows, live while you drag.</figcaption></figure>

Any element can sit beside another. In the Inspector, **Sticks to** picks the element, the
side, the gap and the alignment (a line shows **Connector** with its two ends instead); a
rotated label sits beside it as it looks. Editing a stuck label (its text, bold, size, width or
rotation) keeps it stuck; moving it by hand frees it, and deleting the shape frees what hung on
it. **Settings → Figure → Connectors stick to shapes** turns the sticking off.

From the command line, `flux figure-attach <figure> <element> --start A --end B:e:4` sets a
connector's ends (`<id>[:anchor[:gap]]`), `--to A --side n --gap 8` sits an element beside
another, and `--detach` frees it ([command reference](/docs/commands.html#verb-reference)).

A canvas that holds a stuck element is saved in a newer file format, which older Flux
versions do not open.

## Arranging text in its box {#arranging-text-in-its-box}

Press **T**, then either **click** for a label — the box hugs whatever you type on one line —
or **drag** out a box for a paragraph: the text wraps at the width you drew and the box grows
downward as you type. Every text box has a **sizing** mode you can change later — *Auto*
hugs, *Auto H* wraps at the box width and grows downward, *Fixed* keeps both dimensions — and
everything below arranges the text **inside** that box.

**Align** places the lines across the box: *Left*, *Center*, *Right*, or *Justify*. Justified
text stretches every line out to both edges by widening the gaps **between words** — the
letters keep their own spacing — and leaves the last line of each paragraph at its natural
width, the way a printed column does. A line holding a single long word is left alone, since
there is no gap to widen. It needs a width
to fill, so choosing it on a hugging label turns the label's current width into the box's
width (*Auto H*): nothing moves yet, but drag the box narrower — or keep typing — and the
lines wrap and fill it.

**Vertical** places the block down the box: *Top*, *Middle*, or *Bottom*. The box itself never
moves or changes size — only the text inside it does. There is nothing to see until the box is
taller than the text, so this row appears with *Fixed* sizing (a hugging box is exactly as tall
as its text). It is what lines a label up with the middle of the panel beside it.

**Line height** is the distance between lines, as a multiple of the font size (1.2 by default —
1.5 reads more airily, 1 sets the lines tight). **Paragraph space** adds extra room before each
new paragraph, so you can separate paragraphs without leaving blank lines; it counts only where
you pressed Enter, never between the lines of one wrapped paragraph. **Tracking** is letter
spacing — the space added after every letter. Both are in **points**, like the font size, and a
negative tracking pulls letters together. Tracking changes how much fits on a line, so a
wrapping box re-wraps as you adjust it.

**Halo** puts a ring of the background colour behind the letters, so a label stays readable
where it crosses a plot's lines or an image. Set its width in pixels (0 turns it off); it takes
the figure's or slide's background unless you pick a **Halo colour**. It shows in the editor,
in exported figures and papers, and in slides; PowerPoint text boxes have no halo.

**Italic for one word, not the whole box.** Double-click the text to edit it, select the part
you want — a species name, a gene symbol, a single letter — and press **Ctrl+I**, **Ctrl+B** or
**Ctrl+U**. Only that stretch changes; the box keeps its own font, so the rest of the label is
untouched. With nothing selected, while you are typing, the same keys style only what you type
next: press **Ctrl+I**, type the species name, press **Ctrl+I** again and carry on upright. Moving
the cursor or clicking ends that. To style the whole box, click the box without editing it, or
select all of its text first.

The formatting sticks to the letters it was given: type in the middle of an italic word and the
new letters are italic too, type against its edge and they are not, and deleting the word takes
its formatting with it. The formatting shows on the canvas as you work. Bold makes letters
wider, so after a bold word the text cursor can sit a few pixels off the letters. In the rare
case where a bold word pushes text onto another line, the box shows plain text while you type,
and the bold appears when you click away. (**Escape** throws the whole edit away, formatting
included.)

**Superscript and subscript.** Select the characters and press **Ctrl++** (superscript) or
**Ctrl+=** (subscript), or use the Inspector's **X²** and **X₂** buttons. The characters are set
smaller and raised or lowered, so *x²* and *H₂O* stay in one text box. **Ctrl+.** and **Ctrl+,**
do the same, as in Google Docs. Pressing the same one again puts the characters back on the line,
and with nothing selected it applies to what you type next, like the other styles.

**Colour and the Inspector work on the selected letters too.** While letters are selected, the
Inspector's Text section says *Styling N selected characters*. Its **B**, **I** and **U** buttons
then format just those letters, and you can press several in a row. The *Text* colour swatch
paints just those letters as well, so one symbol can be red inside a black label. Click
**Whole box**, or click the canvas, to style the whole text again. A colormap gradient always
covers the whole box, so it is not offered for a few selected letters.

All of these sit in the Inspector's Text section and in the **F** menu, they apply to every
selected text at once, and each adjustment is one undo step. A **named text style** (the
Inspector's *Style* row) carries them too, so "Panel body, justified, 1.4 line height" becomes
one click on every label in the figure — and editing the style restyles every text linked to
it.

## Cascade {#cascade}

Select several things and press **Ctrl+Shift+C**: the **cascade** popover applies a *stepped
delta* across the selection — each object offset a bit more than the last. Pick the property
(position, rotation, opacity, size, stroke width, font size, or a colour), the step (add or
multiply), and the ordering (selection, layers, left→right, top→bottom); colours ramp
perceptually in OKLCh (ΔL/ΔC/ΔH per step). The preview is live; **Enter** applies as one undo
step, **Escape** puts everything back. Fanned annotations, graded palettes, staircase layouts —
one gesture.

## Reusable designs {#reusable-designs}

**Ctrl+P** opens your **preset library** — a personal, machine-global collection of styled
shapes, arrows, callouts, and whole groups (a badge, a labelled bracket), organized in folders,
inserted with a click. Save anything from the **F** menu's *save as preset*; a group preset
arrives as one unit you can move as one or ungroup.
